The smallest value is \(\boxed{11}\).

To show that \(N\ge 11\), let the first player choose four \(25\)'s, one \(23\), and four \(22\)'s. Their total is
\[
4\cdot25+23+4\cdot22=211.
\]
Every proper subset has sum at most \(211-22=189\), while the whole list has sum \(211\). Hence no subset sum lies in \([190,210]\), so \(N=10\) does not suffice.

Now prove that \(N=11\) always suffices. Order the given list arbitrarily and take the shortest initial segment whose sum \(T\) is at least \(200\). Since the last added number is at most \(25\),
\[
200\le T\le224.
\]
If \(T\le211\), this entire initial segment has sum in \([189,211]\).

Suppose \(212\le T\le224\), and set
\[
L=T-211,
\]
so \(1\le L\le13\). It is enough to find some terms of the initial segment having sum
\[
L\le R\le L+22,
\]
because deleting those terms leaves sum
\[
189=T-(L+22)\le T-R\le T-L=211.
\]

For \(T\ge214\), we have \(L\ge3\). If some term is at least \(L\), that term alone works because it is at most \(25\le L+22\). Otherwise every term is at most \(L-1\); adding terms until their sum first reaches \(L\) gives
\[
L\le R\le2L-2\le L+22.
\]

If \(T=212\), then \(L=1\). Some term is at most \(23\), since a sum of \(212\) cannot be formed entirely from terms \(24\) and \(25\): eight such terms sum to at most \(200\), while nine sum to at least \(216\). That term gives \(1\le R\le23\).

If \(T=213\), then \(L=2\). A term between \(2\) and \(24\) works. If there is no such term, all terms are \(1\) or \(25\). Two \(1\)'s give \(R=2\); with at most one \(1\), however, the total is congruent to \(0\) or \(1\pmod{25}\), whereas \(213\equiv13\pmod{25}\), a contradiction.

Thus a subset sum in \([189,211]\) always exists, proving that \(N=11\) is sufficient and minimal.

The smallest value is \(\boxed{11}\).

First, \(N=10\) does not suffice. Let the first player write five copies of \(23\) and four copies of \(24\). Their total is
\[
5\cdot23+4\cdot24=211.
\]
Every proper subset has sum at most \(211-23=188\), while the entire list has sum \(211\). Hence no subset sum lies in \([190,210]\). Thus every winning value satisfies \(N\ge 11\).

Now consider any finite list of positive integers at most \(25\) whose total is at least \(200\). Among all subsets having sum at least \(189\), choose one that is minimal under inclusion, and denote its sum by \(T\). Such a subset exists because the entire list has sum at least \(200\).

For every selected number \(a\), minimality gives
\[
T-a\le 188.
\]
Since \(a\le25\), it follows that \(T\le213\). We show that \(T\) cannot equal \(212\) or \(213\).

If \(T=213\), then \(T-a\le188\) implies \(a\ge25\) for every selected number. Thus all selected numbers equal \(25\), so their sum is divisible by \(25\), contradicting \(T=213\).

If \(T=212\), then every selected number is at least \(24\), hence is either \(24\) or \(25\). If there are at most eight selected numbers, their sum is at most \(8\cdot25=200\); if there are at least nine, their sum is at least \(9\cdot24=216\). Both alternatives contradict \(T=212\).

Therefore
\[
189\le T\le211,
\]
so the second player can always obtain a sum in \([200-11,200+11]\). Hence \(N=11\) is sufficient, and the lower-bound construction proves it is minimal.

The smallest value is \(\boxed{11}\).

Necessity: Let the first player write four \(25\)'s, one \(23\), and four \(22\)'s. Their total is
\[
4\cdot25+23+4\cdot22=211.
\]
Every proper subset has sum at most \(211-22=189\), while the whole list has sum \(211\). Hence no subset sum lies in \([190,210]\), so \(N=10\) does not suffice. Therefore \(N\ge 11\).

Sufficiency: Consider any permitted list, and suppose for contradiction that it has no subset sum in \([189,211]\). Among all subsets whose sums are at most \(188\), choose one \(B\) with maximal sum \(s\). Since the whole list has sum at least \(200\), some entry \(x\) lies outside \(B\). By maximality, \(s+x>188\); by the supposition, \(s+x\ge212\). Since \(x\le25\), we get \(s\ge187\). Thus \(s\in\{187,188\}\).

If \(s=187\), every entry outside \(B\) equals \(25\). Moreover, \(B\) contains an entry \(b\le23\): otherwise, if \(B\) had at most seven entries its sum would be at most \(7\cdot25=175\), while if it had at least eight its sum would be at least \(8\cdot24=192\). Replacing \(b\) by an outside \(25\) gives the subset sum
\[
187-b+25=212-b\in[189,211],
\]
a contradiction.

Now let \(s=188\). Every outside entry is \(24\) or \(25\), and the same counting argument shows that \(B\) contains an entry \(b\le23\). If some outside entry is \(24\), replacing \(b\) by it gives \(212-b\in[189,211]\).

It remains that every outside entry equals \(25\). The subset \(B\) has a subsubset of sum \(t\in[2,24]\): if an entry lies in \([2,24]\), take it; otherwise all entries are \(1\) or \(25\), and there must be at least two \(1\)'s because \(188\) is neither \(0\) nor \(1\) modulo \(25\). Replacing this subsubset by an outside \(25\) gives
\[
188-t+25=213-t\in[189,211],
\]
again a contradiction.

Consequently every permitted list has a subset sum in \([189,211]\), so \(N=11\) suffices. Together with the construction above, the minimum is \(11\).

problem.theorem: Let \( N \) be a positive integer. Two persons play the following game. The first player writes a list of positive integers not greater than \( 25 \), not necessarily different, such that their sum is at least \( 200 \). The second player wins if he can select some of these numbers so that their sum \( S \) satisfies the condition \( 200-N \leq S \leq 200+N \). What is the smallest value of \( N \) for which the second player has a winning strategy?
